results.Notes: Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0359 (same tranche, the statutory architecture behind the list), and bank items MA-Q-0145 (administration categories at category level), MA-Q-0146 and MA-Q-0147 (MH/SUD prescriber direction and workflow). Materially distinct: MA-Q-0145 works at the level of authorised categories and MA-Q-0328 at the level of the closed product list published in Circular DCP 26-03-124, including the cabotegravir HIV-prevention entry and the 'all salts' testosterone entry that no earlier item reaches. The discriminating work is done by option D, whether the published list is closed or illustrative, and option E, whether administration is compulsory, both of which are judgments rather than recall, so reasoning_not_trivia is satisfied even though options A to C require knowledge of the list itself. Distractors are authentic: generalising from named products to their pharmacological class is the error the circular's own 'only medications eligible' wording is designed to prevent. TRANCHE-LEVEL OBSERVATIONS, recorded once here for the controller rather than against each item. (1) Distribution is healthy. All 35 items sit in area 2 across 23 rule records, 12 carrying a two-item pair and 11 a single item; SBA key positions run A4 B3 C3 D6 E5 over 21 items, which is well balanced and does not repeat the E-heavy concentration flagged in BATCH3-B3B; SATA cardinality runs 2 six times, 3 five times and 4 three times, in line with the 152-item SATA bank. (2) No duplication. Maximum lexical overlap against the whole 406-record bank is 0.28 Jaccard and every top neighbour is an intended same-family sibling. The three places where a tranche item shares a rule record or statutory paragraph with an existing bank item are all complementary rather than repetitive: MA-Q-0311 with MA-Q-0371 on constitution versus currency, MA-Q-0322 with MA-Q-0323 on the exception versus the rest period, and MA-Q-0340 and MA-Q-0341 with MA-Q-0082, MA-Q-0083 and MA-Q-0084 on different limbs of M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5). That paragraph now carries five bank items, which is the densest concentration on any single provision and is worth watching before more are added, but no two of the five ask the same question. (3) A construction signature runs across the four-correct SATA items. In MA-Q-0328, MA-Q-0346 and MA-Q-0359 the single incorrect option is in each case the one that over-generalises, adds an external gate, or asserts uniformity, while every specific, hedged option is keyed correct. A candidate who learns the heuristic 'reject the sweeping option and take the rest' recovers the exact key in all three without reading the authority. MA-Q-0359 is failed on this ground because there the heuristic is sufficient on its own; MA-Q-0328 and MA-Q-0346 survive only because their remaining options still carry content that has to be known. The set would be stronger if at least one four-correct item placed a plausible, specifically worded error among the options instead of relying on a blanket statement to carry the distractor role. (4) Two items are failed for a mis-keyed correct option, MA-Q-0340 option E and MA-Q-0348 option D. Both errors run the same way: a correct statement of a regulation has been recorded as a distractor on a reading that adds a condition the option does not contain. In each case the item contradicts its own governing rule record, and in MA-Q-0340 it also contradicts sibling item MA-Q-0344 in this same tranche. Whatever process produced these two should be checked against the rest of B3-D before release, since the failure mode is a systematic one rather than a slip.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0344 (same tranche, which administration route the facts engage) and bank items MA-Q-0146 and MA-Q-0173. Materially distinct: MA-Q-0146 tests that product eligibility does not supply patient-specific prescriber direction, whereas this item tests a setting limit and the instrument that goes with it. The scenario is a routine community-pharmacy request and the distractors are the two things a competent pharmacist would actually rely on, a valid prescription and completed training with current CPR certification, both of which the circular's OTP note defeats. Good separation between competence and authority.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0147 (bank, the record-sending limb of the same Pharmacist-Prescriber Communication section) and MA-Q-0146. Materially distinct: no existing item tests what follows when the administration notation is absent. The item turns on reading 'should' and 'is encouraged' as hortatory rather than mandatory, which is a genuine interpretive judgment, and the four distractors each convert the guidance into a different hard requirement, which is the realistic error.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0332 (same family, the single-dose condition) and MA-Q-0328. No bank precursor tests the route limitation. Distractors are authentic because an intravenous option premised on the pharmacist's own line-placement training, and a 'any parenteral route the label allows' option, are exactly the inferences a clinically confident candidate makes; the circular closes both. Keying both D and E requires the reader to hold the labeling condition and the route condition together rather than choosing between them.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0331 (same family) and bank item MA-Q-0147, whose related_facts note that eligible products are prescribed in single doses and supplied in single-dose packaging. Materially distinct: MA-Q-0147 states the condition, while this item tests the words 'with or without refills' that follow it, which no bank item reaches. The manager-versus-pharmacist framing is a realistic Massachusetts workflow dispute and the distractors track the plausible misreading that single-dose prescribing excludes repetition.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0334 (same family, the setting boundary) and bank item MA-Q-0123. Materially distinct: this is the only item in the bank that identifies the instrument a collaborating pharmacist must use inside a licensed facility. The scenario, a pharmacist rounding in a long-term care facility leaving a prescription at the nurses' station, is an authentic Massachusetts consultant-pharmacy situation, and the countersignature and oral-order distractors are the habits a candidate imports from other settings.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0333 (same family, the affirmative instrument) and bank items MA-Q-0293 and MA-Q-0294. Materially distinct: it is the paired negative case, testing the licensed-facility boundary rather than the instrument. Assisted living is a well-chosen setting because it genuinely looks like a facility and keeps care records, so option B is a real trap, and option E is a plausible over-correction that the regulation does not support.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0336 (same family, the precondition on the power) and bank item MA-Q-0299. Materially distinct: no existing item addresses the procurement channel for immediate-treatment stock. The item is a genuine legal judgment because the reader must notice that the channel turns on the schedule rather than on prescribing authority, and the Schedule IV option is an authentic trap precisely because Schedule IV feels low-risk while sitting inside the closed II to V band.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0335 (same family) and MA-Q-0339. Materially distinct: it isolates the proviso that ties dispensing for immediate treatment to prescribing authority. Option B, resting on Schedule VI being the least restricted schedule, is an authentic distractor because schedule-based reasoning is the habitual shortcut; the item is not a schedule flashcard because the schedule is precisely what does not answer the question.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0340 (same tranche, retail powers) and bank items MA-Q-0297 and MA-Q-0300 on agreement content and delegation. Materially distinct: no bank item tests whether authority to modify implies authority to discontinue. The distractors are strong because option B's 'stopping is a lesser step than modifying' is genuinely persuasive clinical reasoning, and option C's clinical-not-prescribing framing is the argument a pharmacist would actually advance.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0339 (same family, the federal limb) and bank item MA-Q-0292, which works 247 CMR 16.02(1)(f). Materially distinct: MA-Q-0292 asks what the agreement must contain, while this item asks what a registration obtained for a different purpose does not cover. The scenario is realistic because most pharmacists do hold a Department registration through the pharmacy, and option A is the answer nearly every practitioner would give.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0338 (same family) and MA-Q-0336. Materially distinct: it tests the conditional words 'if applicable' by contrasting two pharmacists, which no bank item does. The two-actor construction forces a real distinction rather than recall, and options A and B are authentic because each applies the cross-reference uniformly, which is the common error.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0341 (same family, the 30-day extension limb), MA-Q-0344 (same tranche, the collaborative vaccine route), and bank items MA-Q-0082, MA-Q-0083 and MA-Q-0084, which already work the same statutory paragraph for referral scope, the Schedule II-V prohibition and initial Schedule VI prescribing. Materially distinct in subject: this is the only item that asks the reader to enumerate the retail powers as a set. FAILS authentic_distractors. Option E, 'She may administer vaccines under the terms of her agreement', is a correct statement of 247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) that has been placed among the distractors, so a well-prepared candidate is penalised for knowing the rule, and the item contradicts MA-Q-0344 and rule MA-CDTM-VACCINE-ADMINISTRATION, which key that proposition as correct. The choice_analysis for option B likewise denies a retail initiation power that MA-Q-0084 and 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)4. both rely on. The construction defect is the mis-keying, not the scenario; see the legal record for the provision analysis and the proposed key A, C, E.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0340 (same family, the powers as a set) and bank item MA-Q-0083, which tests the Schedule II-V prohibition in the same paragraph. Materially distinct: this item isolates the continuation power. Option A is an authentic distractor because initiating an equivalent agent is the clinically sensible response that the statute does not confer, and the stem's detail that the pharmacist has never dispensed this patient a different medication for the condition is doing real work in closing it off. Note for the controller that the core_reasoning wording 'not a power to start something new' is sound about the extension limb but should not be read across to deny the separate retail initial-prescription power, as recorded in the legal record for MA-Q-0340.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0343 (same family, the ambulatory condition). No bank precursor maps the approval authorities. Materially distinct and a genuine judgment, because the reader must resist the single system-wide approval that a real health system would want. Option A is authentic because Department approval is a plausible guess for a licensed hospital, and option B is authentic because it is the operationally attractive answer.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0342 (same family) and bank items MA-Q-0303 and MA-Q-0306. Materially distinct: it tests the cumulative nature of approval and on-site supervision. The remote-pharmacist facts are highly realistic post-2020 practice, and option C, physician reachability during clinic hours, is the strongest possible distractor because it is what most compliance officers would treat as sufficient.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0329 and MA-Q-0349 (same tranche, the other two administration routes) and MA-Q-0340 option E. Materially distinct: this is the only item that asks which of the three Massachusetts administration routes a given set of facts engages. Distractors are authentic because options C and D each import a condition from a genuinely existing neighbouring pathway. The item is correct as keyed; the tranche's problem is that MA-Q-0340 keys the same proposition the other way, which is recorded against that item rather than this one.

Closest comparisons: bank items MA-Q-0095 and MA-Q-0096, which work other limbs of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F, and MA-Q-0402. Materially distinct: neither bank item touches the appointment prohibition. Lexical overlap with the whole bank is the lowest in the tranche at 0.12 Jaccard. The scenario is an entirely realistic pharmacy staffing decision and the distractors are graded concessions, a seven-day slot and a weekly walk-in day, which is a good construction because each is a compromise a real pharmacy would propose.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0347 (same family, the timing duty) and bank items MA-Q-0095 and MA-Q-0096. Materially distinct: the bank items address prior-prescription access and the follow-up clinical visit, while this item addresses the post-prescribing duties in s. 19F(c)(i)(C) to (E). Options A and B are correctly keyed together as the two limbs of one disjunctive duty, and option D is an authentic distractor because a prescriber sign-off is exactly the safeguard readers expect to find. One wording observation that does not affect the key: because the stem has the pharmacist already dispensing, option E states a duty that on these facts has been discharged rather than one newly attaching; asking which duties the statute imposes on the transaction would read more cleanly.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0346 (same family) and bank item MA-Q-0096. Materially distinct: it is the applied case of the dispense-as-soon-as-practicable duty. The Friday-afternoon facts with an equivalent product in stock are well chosen because they remove every practical excuse, and option A, separating the prescribing duty from the dispensing decision, is the argument a pharmacy would actually make.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0349 (same family, the student limb) and MA-Q-0350 (the written-protocol subjects), with no bank precursor on the Commissioner-order gate. FAILS authentic_distractors. Option D, 'Administration must accord with the Commissioner's order as well as a practitioner instrument', restates 105 CMR 700.003(F)(1)(b) as a necessary condition and is a correct statement placed among the distractors. The item is internally inconsistent about this: its own choice_analysis for option C and its reasoning_steps both assert that a practitioner instrument is still required, which is exactly what option D says. Options A and C are genuinely tempting absolutes and would carry the item on their own once D is moved into the key; see the legal record and the proposed key B, D, E.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0348 (same family, the gate) and MA-Q-0350. Materially distinct: it isolates the student limb. Option C, that a student may never administer under this pathway, is an authentic distractor because it is the cautious answer, and option A is authentic because students routinely act on a licensee's authority in other contexts. A genuine reading of 105 CMR 700.003(F)(1)(c) is required.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0348 and MA-Q-0349 (same emergency-vaccine cluster) and bank items MA-Q-0275 and MA-Q-0284. The subject matter is distinct and the key is legally correct. FAILS on construction. The two excluded options are 'Marketing of the vaccination service to patients' and 'Reimbursement arrangements for administered doses', both commercial subjects that no reader would expect in a Department clinical protocol list; they self-eliminate on register alone, and once they go the three remaining options are the whole key, so the item is recoverable from the options' own wording without any knowledge of 105 CMR 700.003(F)(2)(b). It also FAILS reasoning_not_trivia, because every option is a bare 'is this subject named in the paragraph' recall with no legal judgment to make. The author's own note that return of vaccine 'is the subject most often missed' identifies the discrimination the item should be testing but does not currently reach it. Suggested repair: replace the two commercial options with plausible clinical or governance subjects that the paragraph nonetheless omits, such as a requirement to obtain written informed consent for each dose or to report every administration to the immunisation registry within 24 hours, so that the reader must actually work the list.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0352 (same family, the comparative case) and bank item MA-Q-0405. Materially distinct: no bank item tests the outpatient pharmacist's safe harbour. The distractors are unusually good because options A and B state the standard most readers assume applies, that an available record imputes knowledge and that failing to check is negligent, and the statute deliberately does not adopt it. The item requires the reader to notice a legislated departure from the ordinary standard of care.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0351 (same family, the single-actor case). Materially distinct and the harder of the pair: it requires holding two standards from one section apart and applying each to the right professional. Option C, which reverses them, is the authentic trap, and option D, turning the answer on patient harm, is realistic because harm is where most readers expect liability to start. Among the strongest constructions in the tranche.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0354 (same family, the applied case). The 0.27 Jaccard neighbour MA-Q-0380 is a controlled-substance container-label item and shares only generic pharmacy vocabulary, not subject matter. Materially distinct: no bank item lists the pharmacist-prescriber identification particulars. Option E is a genuinely tempting distractor because patient consent really is required in the community pharmacy setting, just not as part of this transmission, and the home-versus-work address discrimination is a fair reading test.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0353 (same family, the list) and bank item MA-Q-0143. Materially distinct: it is the applied decision on an incomplete transmission. The construction is good because the caller supplies four of the five particulars, so the reader must check against the list rather than judge whether the missing item feels important, which is exactly the stated trap. Option D is authentic because many readers assume a pharmacist may not telephone a prescription at all.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0356 (same family, the comparative case) and bank item MA-Q-0201. Materially distinct: no bank item works the structure of the s. 9(a) practitioner list. The item is genuine statutory reading rather than recall, since options C and D are the two available readings of the same 'as limited by' clause and only one survives. Option E is authentic because good faith is the more memorable condition and readers routinely treat it as the operative one.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0355 (same family). Materially distinct and the harder of the pair: it puts a pharmacist and a physician on identical registration footing so that only the statutory qualifier separates them. The two-actor construction is realistic for a shared clinic and the distractors are well graded, with option C reversing the asymmetry and option D denying the possession authority outright.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0358 (same family, the confidentiality limb) and bank items MA-Q-0318 and MA-Q-0391. Materially distinct: no bank item compares the three standing-order reporting cadences. Option A, a single combined annual return, is an authentic distractor because it is what any pharmacy would actually want, and option D is authentic because it mirrors the COVID-19 regime onto emergency contraception. Requires holding three statutes side by side rather than recalling one.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0357 (same family) and bank item MA-Q-0316. Materially distinct: it tests public-record status rather than cadence. The journalist framing is a realistic Massachusetts public-records scenario, and option B, release with patient identifiers redacted, is the strongest distractor because redaction is the ordinary answer under the public records law and the statute here removes the filings from that regime entirely.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0328 (same tranche, the product list under the same architecture) and bank item MA-Q-0145, which tests pharmacist-administration categories at category level. Materially distinct in subject: this is the only item in the 406-record bank that asks the reader to separate the three clauses of the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 definition by their differing gates, and the key is legally correct. FAILS wording_not_guessable. Four of the five options are keyed correct and the single distractor, option A, is the one blanket assertion that all three routes 'rest on the same statutory clause and share the same conditions'. Options B through E visibly describe different gates for different routes, so they are jointly inconsistent with A, and a reader with no knowledge of the statute can reject A on internal consistency alone and then select the remaining four. Suggested repair: replace one of the four correct options with a plausible but wrong gate, for example that the gender-affirming testosterone route additionally requires departmental regulations, so that the reader must attribute the regulation gate to the correct clause rather than merely spot the odd one out.

Closest comparisons: MA-Q-0311 and bank item MA-Q-0371 on agreement currency, and MA-Q-0298. Materially distinct: it is the only item in the bank turning on the supervising physician's controlled-substance status. Distractors are authentic because options B, C and D each rest on a real and reassuring fact, an unrestricted medical licence, the absence of notice and the state-versus-federal distinction, and the regulation defeats each. Option E, confining herself to non-controlled therapies, is the most tempting because it sounds like proportionate risk management. Strong item.

Closest comparisons: bank item MA-Q-0371, which shares the family identifier CPA_VALID_CONSTITUTION_AND_BIENNIAL_CURRENCY and the same rule record, and MA-Q-0300. Materially distinct rather than duplicative: MA-Q-0311 tests what makes an agreement validly constituted and MA-Q-0371 tests whether a validly constituted agreement remains current at twenty-six months, and MA-Q-0371's own trap note is written to pair with it. Option D, a filing requirement, is an authentic distractor because filing genuinely is required in analogous licensure processes and 247 CMR 16.04(6) requires retention without filing.

Closest comparisons: bank item MA-Q-0323, which shares the family identifier PRACTICE_HOUR_CEILING_AND_REST_PERIOD and the same rule record, and MA-Q-0376. Materially distinct rather than duplicative: MA-Q-0322 tests the conditions attaching to the extenuating-circumstance exception and MA-Q-0323 tests the eight consecutive hour rest requirement on the way back. Option D is an outstanding distractor because a district manager's instruction is the real-world pressure the regulation is meant to withstand, and option E is authentic because many pharmacy rules genuinely do distinguish technicians. The item is a fitness-to-practise judgment, not a numeric flashcard, because the number is given and the conditions are the point.
